prompt.context: Strong Steel Co. is a large European steel manufacturing company with annual revenues of $6.3B and operating profits of $650M. The company operates integrated mills. Their competitors in Europe are 10 other integrated mills (IMs), using 150-year-old blast furnace technology, and 30 mini-mills (MMs), all of which are smaller than the IMs and use the most modern technology, commercialized during the 1970s. Both types of mills go through Cast, Melt, Roll, Finish, and Coat stages, but only the melting process differs: integrated mills use ore/coke/coal with a basic oxygen furnace and blast furnace, while mini-mills use scrap with an electric arc furnace. Products at successive stages: Melt, Slab, Hot Roll, Cold Roll, Hot Dip, Electro-galvanized.
prompt.question: A new steel commodity exchange is under development in the European Union. The company will be able to buy and sell commodity steel (hot rolls) on the exchange. With the opening of the online exchange, should Strong Steel Co. continue to make its own commodity steel (hot rolls) or should it buy commodity steel from the exchange? If they exit commodity steel production, the purchased hot rolls would be used as inputs for manufacturing value-added steel.

clarifying_info.q: What products does Strong Steel currently produce and in what volumes?
clarifying_info.a: Hot roll: 13,000 tons at $275/ton, unit cost $260/ton. Cold roll: 5,000 tons at $320/ton, unit cost $280/ton. Hot dipped: 2,000 tons at $410/ton, unit cost $360/ton. Electro-galvanized: 1,000 tons at $560/ton, unit cost $475/ton. Total volume: 21,000 tons.

clarifying_info.q: What are mini-mill production costs for commodity steel?
clarifying_info.a: Mini-mills produce commodity steel (hot rolls) at $220 per ton operating cost.

clarifying_info.q: What happens to the commodity steel if Strong Steel stops producing it?
clarifying_info.a: They would buy hot rolls from the exchange to use as inputs for their value-added products (cold roll, hot dipped, electro-galvanized).

exhibits.title: Process Flow Diagram
exhibits.shows: A side-by-side process flow for integrated mills and mini-mills, showing the stages (Cast, Melt, Roll, Finish, Coat) and the product at each stage (Melt, Slab, Hot Roll, Cold Roll, Hot Dip, Electro-galvanized). Only the Melt stage differs between the two mill types.
exhibits.data: Integrated mill inputs: Ore, Coke, Coal via Basic oxygen furnace + Blast furnace. Mini-mill inputs: Scrap via Electric arc furnace. Shared downstream: Continuous caster, Hot rolling line, Cold rolling line, Hot dipping line, Electro-galvanizing line.

framework: Understand the current revenue and profit contribution of commodity steel (hot rolls) vs. value-added steel
Assess the cost competitiveness of Strong Steel in commodity steel production relative to mini-mills
Estimate the likely market price of hot rolls on the exchange (driven by low-cost mini-mill producers)
Determine how much per-ton savings from buying on the exchange are needed to offset the profit given up
Weigh risks of exiting commodity steel production

questions.prompt: What does the process flow diagram tell you about the two mill types?
questions.guidance: Only the melting process differs between integrated mills and mini-mills. All downstream processes (casting, rolling, finishing, coating) are identical. The basic product at each stage gains value: Hot Roll feeds downstream value-added processing.

questions.prompt: Calculate revenue, operating costs, operating profit, revenue as % of total, and profit as % of total for each product line.
questions.guidance: Commodity steel (hot roll) contributes over half of revenue but only one-third of profits, indicating relatively low margins. Value-added products are more profitable. The candidate should recognize that exiting commodity steel would sacrifice $195M in profit but account for more than half of current revenue.

math.setup: Volume (000 tons) x Price ($/ton) = Sales ($M); Volume x Unit Cost = Operating Costs ($M); Sales - Costs = Operating Profit ($M)
steps: Hot roll: 13,000 x $275 = $3,575M revenue; 13,000 x $260 = $3,380M costs; profit = $195M; revenue share = 3575/6555 = 54.54%; profit share = 195/580 = 33.62%
Cold roll: 5,000 x $320 = $1,600M; 5,000 x $280 = $1,400M; profit = $200M; rev share = 24.41%; profit share = 34.48%
Hot dipped: 2,000 x $410 = $820M; 2,000 x $360 = $720M; profit = $100M; rev share = 12.51%; profit share = 17.24%
Electro-galvanized: 1,000 x $560 = $560M; 1,000 x $475 = $475M; profit = $85M; rev share = 8.54%; profit share = 14.66%
math.answer: Commodity steel (hot roll): $3,575M sales, $3,380M costs, $195M profit (54.54% of revenue, 33.62% of profit). Value-added total: $2,980M sales, $2,595M costs, $385M profit. Grand total: $6,555M revenue, $5,975M costs, $580M profit.

questions.prompt: Given that mini-mills produce hot rolls at $220/ton versus Strong Steel's $260/ton cost, what is the likely direction of the exchange price for hot rolls?
questions.guidance: Mini-mills have a $40/ton cost advantage over integrated mills. In a competitive commodity exchange, prices will be driven toward the marginal cost of the low-cost producer (mini-mills at $220/ton). This means the exchange price is likely to fall below $260/ton — Strong Steel's current cost — making in-house production of hot rolls a loss-making activity at market prices.

math.setup: Compare Strong Steel unit cost vs. mini-mill unit cost
steps: Strong Steel hot roll unit cost: $260/ton
If exchange price converges toward $220-$260/ton, Strong Steel's margin on hot rolls erodes or goes negative
math.answer: Exchange price likely to fall below $260/ton; Strong Steel would incur losses producing commodity steel at current costs.

questions.prompt: If Strong Steel exits commodity steel production and buys hot rolls from the exchange for its value-added operations, what is the minimum per-ton saving required to maintain current total profit?
questions.guidance: The candidate must calculate the profit given up by exiting hot roll production, then divide by the volume of value-added steel that would consume the purchased hot rolls. This gives the required per-ton cost saving from buying on the exchange versus implied internal cost.

math.setup: Profit foregone from exiting hot rolls / Volume of value-added steel remaining
steps: Profit to give up: $195M (hot roll operating profit)
Value-added tons remaining: 5,000 (cold roll) + 2,000 (hot dipped) + 1,000 (electro-galvanized) = 8,000 tons
Required saving per ton: $195,000,000 / 8,000 = $24,375 per ton
math.answer: Strong Steel needs at least approximately $24–$25 per ton saving on purchased hot rolls to maintain current total profit levels.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the key risks if Strong Steel exits commodity steel production and begins buying hot rolls from the exchange?

categories.name: Labor & Social
ideas: Union backlash and labor disputes from workforce reductions
Government pressure to protect steel industry jobs
Regulatory or political obstacles to plant closures

categories.name: Operational & Quality
ideas: Loss of control over hot roll quality used as inputs
Supply disruptions affecting downstream value-added production
Dependency on exchange availability and liquidity

categories.name: Financial & Market
ideas: Exposure to commodity price volatility on the exchange
Risk that exchange prices rise above current internal cost of $260/ton
Reduced bargaining power as a buyer rather than integrated producer

categories.name: Competitive
ideas: Competitors who remain integrated could use cheap hot rolls as a weapon
Strategic weakness if exchange liquidity dries up

recommendation: Strong Steel should exit commodity steel (hot roll) production and buy from the exchange
Mini-mills have a $40/ton cost advantage; exchange prices will likely fall below Strong Steel's $260/ton cost, turning in-house production into a loss-making activity
The required $24–$25/ton saving from exchange purchases is achievable given the mini-mill cost advantage, allowing Strong Steel to maintain profits while eliminating unprofitable commodity production
Exiting hot rolls also frees capital and management focus for higher-margin value-added products
risks: Labor and union disruptions from plant closures
Loss of quality control over hot roll inputs
Exposure to commodity price volatility on the exchange
Supply risk if exchange liquidity is insufficient
next_steps: Negotiate transition plan with unions and government
Identify reliable exchange counterparties and establish supply contracts
Assess capital redeployment options for freed blast furnace assets
Monitor exchange price trends to validate the buy decision over time
